theme: The resurrection, “He is risen; he is not here”
readingInstruction: Read Mark 16:1-20. The women find the empty tomb. Note that the earliest manuscripts end at verse 8, and verses 9 to 20 are not found in them. Many Bible translations set those verses apart. Read verses 1 to 8 as Mark’s own ending, and then the longer ending as an early summary of the resurrection appearances and the commission.
settingTheScene: After the Sabbath, early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bring spices to anoint Jesus’ body. Their question on the way is practical: who will roll the stone away? What they find is an empty tomb and a young man in a white robe. The abrupt ending at verse 8 is deliberate: it leaves the reader to respond. The longer ending (vv. 9 to 20) was added early and summarizes appearances recorded elsewhere.
observation: “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” (16:3).
“They saw that the stone had been rolled back” (16:4).
“Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him” (16:6).
“But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee” (16:7).
“And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid” (16:8).
“Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation” (16:15).
“So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God” (16:19).
“And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs” (16:20).
interpretation:
The women wonder how they will move the large stone, and when they look up, they see that it has already been rolled back. Inside the tomb, a young man sits on the right side, dressed in a white robe. The women are alarmed. He says, “Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here.” The One who was crucified is the One who is risen. He points to the place where they laid him, empty. Then he gives a message: “Go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.” Notice “and Peter.” The disciple who denied him is not cast aside. He is specifically named.

Then, in the oldest manuscripts, the Gospel ends: “And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.” It is an abrupt ending, but it is powerful. After all that the disciples have done, the final faithful ones, the women, are also afraid. The reader is left with the announcement of the resurrection and the question: what will you do with this? We know the women did tell, because otherwise there would be no Gospel. The book ends where it began, with the good news, and invites us to carry it forward.

Verses 9 to 20, the longer ending, were probably added early. They summarize the appearance to Mary Magdalene, to two disciples on the road, and to the eleven, and give the commission: “Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.” It ends with Jesus’ ascension and the disciples preaching everywhere with the Lord working with them. Because the status of these verses is uncertain, Christians are wise not to build doctrine or practice on them alone. In particular, the verses about handling serpents and drinking poison (vv. 17 to 18) are not taught elsewhere in the New Testament as normative. The commission itself is confirmed in Matthew 28 and Acts 1.

The resurrection is the proof of everything Jesus said. His claim to be the Christ, his death as a ransom, his promise to rise, all are vindicated. The strong Son of God who died as a servant is alive.
connection: Psalm 16:10 and Isaiah 53:10-12 foreshadow the resurrection. Mark 8:31, 9:31, and 10:34 are the three predictions. Mark 14:28 promised he would go before them to Galilee. Matthew 28, Luke 24, and John 20 give the other resurrection accounts. 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 lists the appearances. Acts 1:8-11 records the commission and ascension. Romans 1:4 says he was declared to be the Son of God by his resurrection. 1 Peter 1:3 says we have a living hope through the resurrection.
application:
Say aloud, “He has risen; he is not here.” Let it settle.

Notice the words “and Peter.” Hear Jesus naming you in his forgiveness after your failures.

Don’t stay silent out of fear. Think of one person you can tell about the resurrection this week.
prayerPrompts: Praise Jesus that he is not in the tomb.
Thank him that the empty tomb proves his work is finished.
Ask him to send you to tell someone.
